title: 2  Ubuntu general guidelines
text:
2.2 Ubuntu file and package structure

2.2.1 System-wide location (for core programs)
System-wide locations affect all users. Software is installed with sudo, on the root of the system.










Location
Purpose




/usr/bin
System executables (APT)


/etc
System-wide configuration (example: define repositories for apt)


/opt
Vendor (external) apps


/usr/local/bin
Admin-installed software


/var
Logs, caches, databases





Table 2.1: Main system-wide software locations




/opt for third-party application bundles, self-contained, while /usr/local is for third-party binaries. Besides, /opt is not in the path by default.



2.2.2 User-specific locations
The user does not require root.










Location
Purpose




~/Applications
AppImages


~/.local/bin
User executables


~/scripts/tools
Custom bash executables


~/.local/share
User app data, notably ~/.local/share/applications storing desktop icons


~/.config
User configuration





Table 2.2: Main user-based software locations, to be compared with Table 2.1










Figure 2.1: Detailed structure of Ubuntu package layout









NoteSpecific folders






usr folder stores read-only executables, while /var is regularly written upon changes:

/var/lib: apt and dpkg databases, for instance, respectively stored under dpkg, and /apt
/var/cache: metadata caches for faster execution

/usr/local/, or $HOME/.local stores executables that require custom compilation with make, or qmake, rendered from manual archives:

bin, sbin for executables
share for icons (under subfolder icons) and desktop configuration, documentation under /doc
lib for extensions of a given executable (such as packages in R, or modules in Python)
This folder hierarchy follows the XDG Base Directory Specification

/tmp for temporary folders, cleaned after reboot
/run for sockets, namely used for controlling all the protocols running in the background for connecting to a server, such as the ssh-agent
~/.config/systemd: lists all processes that keep on running in the background, such as Cursor updates, or OneDrive synchronisations.

title: 2  Ubuntu general guidelines
text:
2.3 Recommended updating policy of Ubuntu

Use the maintained helper script ubuntu/update_os.sh. It runs the usual apt update / upgrade / cleanup path, but refuses kernel package changes when any installed DKMS module is missing or broken for the running (or newest) kernel — so a partial upgrade cannot leave you without drivers such as webcam relays, NVIDIA, or VirtualBox.
Make it executable and run it with admin rights:



Listing 2.2: Run the Ubuntu update helper


chmod +x ubuntu/update_os.sh
sudo ./ubuntu/update_os.sh



To force a kernel upgrade anyway (only if you accept a broken DKMS stack): sudo FORCE_KERNEL_UPGRADE=1 ./ubuntu/update_os.sh.
Reboot the system with reboot when a new kernel was installed.







CautionUbuntu partial updates






Partial updates breaking key driver components occur more often with Ubuntu compared to Microsoft, since Linux tends to provide lots of separate, modular packages while Windows ships large and standalone bundles — Consequence: more issues with updates, especially if the network connection dropped, and the newest versions of the packages were not fully installed.



General recommendations:

# to be run daily
sudo apt update
sudo apt upgrade

# to be run monthly
sudo apt full-upgrade

## clean deprecated dependencies
sudo apt autoremove
sudo apt autoclean


Deal with driver issues

## Check for Broken Packages
sudo dpkg --configure -a
## Install missing dependencies
sudo apt -f install

## List all Hardware Driver Errors
dmesg -l err,crit,alert,emerg

section: 2.4 Monitor processes running in the background, and on startup
text:
2.4 Monitor processes running in the background, and on startup

systemctl list-unit-files --type=service --state=running --user to list all processes running in the background, even after rebooting, restrained to the user-level.

Alternatively, processes at the system-level are stored under /lib/systemd/system/

systemctl status <service> retrieves current status

title: 2  Ubuntu general guidelines
text:
2.5 Network protocols, and connection troubleshoots

Two IP protocols for Wi-Fi: IPv4 versus IPv6.







TipThe two Internet protocols, namely IPv4 vs IPv6



IPv4 is older, but still prevailing in many websites, such as GitHub, or OneDrive:

Uses 32-bit addresses (e.g. 192.168.1.10)
Used by most websites, CDNs, VPNs, corporate services
But the 32-bit limitation hinders the number of available IP addresses.

IPv6 is newer, but not universally supported:

Uses 128-bit addresses (e.g. 2a01:cb14:86a7::1)
Supported by modern ISPs and operating systems
Some networks provide IPv6-only, with no IPv4 fallback. Especially the case with Microsoft services, governmental or academic websites.




You can test if this is the issue to connect to some websites with curl <webdomain>, such as curl https://onedrive.live.com, returning Cannot connect
Recent modern routers return only IPv6 — while Windows is able to auto-fall back to IPv4, this is not the case of IPv6.

Temporary fix: by running the following instructions, you solve this issue by automatically configuring an IPv4 upon failure. Recommended only for short-term debugging.

# install dhclient
sudo dhclient -4 wlp2s0f0 <Wifi-name> ## in my case, wlp2s0f0
2.6 Eduroam connection


Ensure to delete beforehand any pre-existing installation: rm -rf $HOME/.config/cat_installer.
Go to https://cat.eduroam.org/, the website usually provides with the version fitting your OS distribution.
On Linux, download the Python script, choosing AMU university.
Run Python script with python3 eduroam-linux-AUA.py
As userid, provide your academic mail address, and as password, your ENT password.

section: 2.7 Pimp your shell: switch from boring Bash to fancy Zsh
text:
2.7 Pimp your shell: switch from boring Bash to fancy Zsh

Installation script:




Listing 2.3: Install Zsh, set it as default shell, and install Oh My Zsh


sudo apt update
sudo apt install zsh

## change the default shell shebang
chsh -s $(which zsh) ## modify /etc/passwd repository
reboot # required log out for effective changes

## check if zsh is used by default (also the theme is modified)
getent passwd "$USER" # returns "/home/bastien:/usr/bin/zsh"

## Install advanced customisation of the shell with Oh My Zsh addon
sh -c "$(curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ohmyzsh/ohmyzsh/master/tools/install.sh)" # create automatically the ~/.zshrc configuration file




You should keep the original ~/.bashrc as a fallback for Bash.


Install the modern alternative to ls, namely eza




Listing 2.4: Install eza from the community APT repository


# install the gpg command
sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y gpg

# install eza
wget -qO- https://raw.githubusercontent.com/eza-community/eza/main/deb.asc | sudo gpg --dearmor -o /etc/apt/keyrings/gierens.gpg
echo "deb [signed-by=/etc/apt/keyrings/gierens.gpg] http://deb.gierens.de stable main" | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/gierens.list
sudo chmod 644 /etc/apt/keyrings/gierens.gpg /etc/apt/sources.list.d/gierens.list
sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y eza




Change the behaviour of the shell:


System-wide: all executables installed under /usr folder can be called directly from the $PATH. For third-party apps stored under /opt, you must add a symlink redirecting to your local folder: sudo ln -s /opt/<appName> /usr/local/bin/<appName>.
User-level: customise .bashrc (and .zshrc if using the .zsh fancy shebang) — Only affects the current user, see my own .zshrc configuration file, and below ls output Figure 2.2.









Modified behaviour of the ls output







Modified behaviour of the ll output, displaying in addition to file names their sizes, permission rights, and original owner









The la output displays in addition to the ll output the hidden files (traditionally starting with a .)







The lt output is a combination of both ls and tree to display the hierarchical structure of a folder






Figure 2.2: Visual representation of my customised ls commands to display the content of a folder from a Bash terminal.

text: 3.1 Git and GitHub configuration

title: 3  Software to install
text:
Figure 3.2: Overview of recommended GitHub security and collaboration practices




GitHub often requires two-factor authentication; set it under https://github.com/settings/security (see also Figure 3.2). Prefer a passkey if your device supports it (Linux often does not), or an authenticator app such as Microsoft Authenticator. Avoid SMS + mobile phone as the sole second factor.
Configure your access to GitHub:


Choose either SSH or HTTPS.
For HTTPS, create one token per device under https://github.com/settings/tokens. Name the token after your laptop, its configuration, and owner. Assign at least the repo and related read scopes. Copy it once — it will not be shown again.


General options to configure:


Use the command line (this also creates ~/.gitconfig):



Listing 3.1: Set global Git identity


git config --global user.name "<your-github-username>"
git config --global user.email "<your.email@example.org>"



Or edit ~/.gitconfig directly (more prone to indentation errors). A default configuration is shown in Listing 3.2; for a fuller description of options, see Formation Git 2024, a tutorial by Benjamin:



Listing 3.2: Example ~/.gitconfig


[user]
  name = <your-github-username>
  email = <your.email@example.org>
## modern default git options
[init]
  defaultBranch = main

## simplifying solving git conflicts + troubleshoot solving
[merge]
  conflictstyle = zdiff3
[rerere]
  enabled = true

## tolerate distinct end of lines
[core]
  autocrlf = input

## visualisation
[tag]
  sort = version:refname
[branch]
  sort = -committerdate
[credential]
  helper = store





Avoid typing your password for every login:


For HTTPS + personal access token (PAT), use git config --global credential.helper store for permanent storage of the credential (consider whether the on-disk store should be encrypted), or git config --global credential.helper 'cache --timeout=3600' for temporary access3.
Or define an SSH key and use the SSH remote URL.

title: 3  Software to install
text:
3.2 PDF management

3.2.1 Sioyek as PDF viewer
Sioyek is an open-source PDF viewer aimed at technical papers with mathematical formulae. Typical uses include coloured highlights (h), smart jumps to figures by clicking them, and bookmarks (b).

Choose a portable build or a standard distribution from the Sioyek releases.
Unzip the archive and make the binary executable with chmod +x.
Run it.







NoteFrom archive to PATH and Start menu: a step-by-step Ubuntu example





To turn an executable into a desktop application on Ubuntu GNOME, follow these steps (paths follow Sioyek; other packages may differ):

Relocate files under /opt/sioyek4.




Listing 3.3: Install Sioyek from archive


## create required folders
sudo mkdir -p /opt/sioyek
sudo mkdir -p /etc/sioyek
sudo mkdir -p /usr/share/sioyek

## relocate, if not already done, the sioyek builds

### core executables
sudo cp ~/sioyek/build/sioyek /opt/sioyek/
sudo chmod +x /opt/sioyek/sioyek

### configuration files
sudo cp ~/sioyek/build/prefs.config /etc/sioyek/
sudo cp ~/sioyek/build/keys.config  /etc/sioyek/
sudo cp -r ~/sioyek/build/shaders /usr/share/sioyek/
sudo cp ~/sioyek/build/tutorial.pdf /usr/share/sioyek/




Add an icon and a GNOME launcher entry:




Listing 3.4: Sioyek desktop entry


sudo mkdir -p /usr/share/icons/hicolor/256x256/apps
## place sioyek.png in that folder (downloaded from the web)

sudo tee /usr/share/applications/sioyek.desktop > /dev/null <<'EOF'
[Desktop Entry]
Version=1.0
Type=Application
Name=Sioyek
GenericName=PDF Viewer
Comment=Fast keyboard-driven PDF viewer
Exec=/opt/sioyek/sioyek %f
Icon=sioyek
Terminal=false
Categories=Office;Viewer;
MimeType=application/pdf;
StartupNotify=true
EOF

## Refresh desktop database
sudo update-desktop-database




(Optional) Make Sioyek the default PDF viewer, using either:

GUI method:

Right-click any PDF.
Properties → Open With.
Select Sioyek.
Click Set as default.

Or the command line:





Listing 3.5: Set Sioyek as default PDF viewer


xdg-mime default sioyek.desktop application/pdf

## to check default
xdg-mime query default application/pdf




Add Sioyek to the PATH via a symbolic link:




Listing 3.6: Symlink Sioyek into PATH


sudo ln -s /opt/sioyek/sioyek /usr/local/bin/sioyek








3.2.2 Sejda for interactive PDF editing

Web version
Sejda add-on for Chrome



3.2.3 PDFtk

Use PDFtk if you prefer editing PDFs from the command line (sudo apt install pdftk when available).

title: 3  Software to install
text:
3.4 LibreOffice

Install the main suite (Writer, Calc, …) with:



Listing 3.9: Install LibreOffice


sudo apt install libreoffice libreoffice-gtk3



Useful extensions (add via Tools → Extensions):

Rotate images in Writer with the Rotate extension.
Install dictionaries and grammar tools (Grammalecte and LanguageTool). Check whether LanguageTool is still worth the resource cost; it is AI-based and can be heavy. You may configure the Java version under Tools → Options → Advanced. Also install the French localisation package:



Listing 3.10: French dictionary for LibreOffice


## French dictionary / hyphenation
sudo apt update
sudo apt install libreoffice-l10n-fr



Install the TeXMaths LaTeX extension.

Font customisation:

Install core Windows fonts:



Listing 3.11: Install Microsoft core fonts


sudo apt update
sudo apt install ttf-mscorefonts-installer ## Microsoft core fonts
fc-cache -f -v ## rebuild font cache so fonts appear in LibreOffice



Extra fonts (or use the native Fonts manager under GNOME). Many popular fonts are available under the Every-Font GitHub repository:



Listing 3.12: Install extra fonts


mkdir -p ~/.local/share/fonts ## ensure personal fonts folder exists
wget -P ~/.local/share/fonts \
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/serendipious/every-font/master/CenturyGothic-Italic%20-%20Century%20Gothic%20-%20Italic.ttf"
fc-cache -f -v ## update font cache











CautionCore typographic options





The main stylistic variants of fonts you can control are:

Weight (Light, Regular, Bold, …)
Angle or shape (regular versus italic)
Width
Serif versus sans-serif. This property is structural to a typeface; for example, Times New Roman is serif, and Century Gothic is sans-serif. For data visualisations or presentations, sans-serif typefaces are usually preferred; the reverse often holds for printed documents.
Advanced options (ligatures, etc.) under LibreOffice → Format → Character → Features (see Figure 3.3).

Make sure, if available, to download at least the regular, bold, italic, and bold-italic versions of each font.







Figure 3.3: Main typographic options

title: 3  Software to install
text:
3.5 Docker

Download dependencies, configuration files, and add the Docker repository to apt for automatic updates (Listing 3.13):




Listing 3.13: Add Docker APT repository


sudo apt update
sudo apt install ca-certificates curl

## Part I: create, download and make Docker apt key readable
sudo install -m 0755 -d /etc/apt/keyrings
sudo curl -fsSL https://download.docker.com/linux/ubuntu/gpg \
  -o /etc/apt/keyrings/docker.asc
sudo chmod a+r /etc/apt/keyrings/docker.asc

## Part II: define where and which Docker packages to install
sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/docker.sources <<EOF
Types: deb
URIs: https://download.docker.com/linux/ubuntu
Suites: $(. /etc/os-release && echo "${UBUNTU_CODENAME:-$VERSION_CODENAME}")
Components: stable
Signed-By: /etc/apt/keyrings/docker.asc
EOF

## Part III: refresh package lists
sudo apt update




Install the Docker toolkit:




Listing 3.14: Install Docker Engine


sudo apt install docker-ce docker-ce-cli containerd.io \
  docker-buildx-plugin docker-compose-plugin




Run Docker without sudo for your main laptop user (Listing 3.15):




Listing 3.15: Allow Docker without sudo


# create a Unix group allowing Docker without admin rights
sudo groupadd docker
# add the current user to it
sudo usermod -aG docker $USER




Check the installation with sudo docker run hello-world. If Docker does not start on login, enable it with sudo systemctl enable --now docker. More detail is in the official Ubuntu install guide.

Useful Docker tutorials:

Benjamin’s presentation
VS Code, R and Docker with Dev Containers
VS Code, Python and Docker with Dev Containers
Dev Containers, from INRIA trainings

title: 3  Software to install
text:
3.6 Web browsers

3.6.1 Firefox

Avoid sudo apt install firefox without first configuring Mozilla’s APT source — the default Ubuntu package may pull in snapd and a Snap-based Firefox.


Import and add the Mozilla APT signing key (Listing 3.16):




Listing 3.16: Add Mozilla Firefox APT key


## Download APT key
wget -q https://packages.mozilla.org/apt/repo-signing-key.gpg -O- \
  | sudo tee /etc/apt/keyrings/packages.mozilla.org.asc > /dev/null

## Add it to the Apt registry
cat <<EOF | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/mozilla.sources
Types: deb
URIs: https://packages.mozilla.org/apt
Suites: mozilla
Components: main
Signed-By: /etc/apt/keyrings/packages.mozilla.org.asc
EOF

## Prefer Mozilla Firefox over Snap packaging
echo '
Package: *
Pin: origin packages.mozilla.org
Pin-Priority: 1000
' | sudo tee /etc/apt/preferences.d/mozilla




Install Firefox from Mozilla:




Listing 3.17: Install Firefox from Mozilla APT


sudo apt update
sudo apt install firefox

which firefox ## should not report a snap path
apt policy firefox





3.6.2 Google Chrome

Download the .deb archive, then install it:




Listing 3.18: Download Google Chrome .deb


sudo apt install ./google-chrome-stable_current_amd64.deb




Add Google’s APT signing key for automatic updates (Listing 3.19):




Listing 3.19: Install Google Chrome


## Download APT key
wget -q -O - https://dl.google.com/linux/linux_signing_key.pub \
  | sudo gpg --dearmor -o /usr/share/keyrings/google-linux-signing-key.gpg

## Add it to the Apt registry
echo "deb [arch=amd64 signed-by=/usr/share/keyrings/google-linux-signing-key.gpg] http://dl.google.com/linux/chrome/deb/ stable main" \
  | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/google-chrome.list

## Update package lists
sudo apt update




Optionally add the Grammarly Chrome plug-in for spelling and grammar checks (pick one regional English variety and stick to it — British English for this course).

text:
3.10 Zotero

Install Java support for the LibreOffice plug-in:




Listing 3.22: Ensure Java for Zotero


sudo apt install libreoffice-java-common -y




Retrieve the latest stable build from https://www.zotero.org/download/6.
Extract and link the executable (Listing 3.23), then install the Zotero Connector in your browser:




Listing 3.23: Extract and link Zotero


#!/bin/bash

## part I: extract archive
sudo tar -xjf zotero.tar.bz2 -C /opt
sudo mv /opt/Zotero_linux-x86_64 /opt/zotero

## Part II: add the executable to PATH
sudo ln -s /opt/zotero/zotero /usr/local/bin/zotero




(Optional) Create a desktop launcher at ~/.local/share/applications/zotero.desktop with the content in Listing 3.24, then make it executable: chmod +x ~/.local/share/applications/zotero.desktop.




Listing 3.24: Zotero desktop entry


[Desktop Entry]
Name=Zotero
Exec=/usr/local/bin/zotero
Icon=/opt/zotero/icons/icon128.png
StartupWMClass=Zotero
Type=Application
Terminal=false
Categories=Office;
MimeType=text/plain;x-scheme-handler/zotero;application/x-research-info-systems;text/x-research-info-systems;text/ris;application/x-endnote-refer;application/x-inst-for-Scientific-info;application/mods+xml;application/rdf+xml;application/x-bibtex;text/x-bibtex;application/marc;application/vnd.citationstyles.style+xml
X-GNOME-SingleWindow=true




Inspired by the Zotero hacks tutorial, keep article files synced across machines while controlling what Zotero stores in the cloud:


Add the plug-ins Better BibTeX (needed for exporting a clean .bib file) and Zotmoov (replaces the older ZotFile extension for filing PDFs by author name).
Edit Zotero preferences7:

Uncheck automatic web-page snapshots (reduces clutter from many small files).
Uncheck full-text sync.
Under Edit → Settings → Advanced, keep separate:

the base directory (the folder synced by your file sharing software), and
a custom data directory in a different location, managed by Zotero itself (Figure 3.4).










Figure 3.4: Zotero advanced database configuration



iii. Configure **Better BibTeX** citation keys the same way on every
     machine (for example
     `[auth:lower][year][journal:lower:abbr]`).

text:
3.11 Quarto, R and Cursor

3.11.1 R and recommended packages

To get recent R builds, add the CRAN signing key and repository (Listing 3.25). Adjust the Ubuntu codename (jammy, noble, …) to match your release:




Listing 3.25: Add CRAN APT repository for R


sudo mkdir -p /etc/apt/keyrings
sudo wget -O /etc/apt/keyrings/cran.gpg \
  https://cloud.r-project.org/bin/linux/ubuntu/marutter_pubkey.asc
echo "deb [signed-by=/etc/apt/keyrings/cran.gpg] https://cloud.r-project.org/bin/linux/ubuntu jammy-cran40/" \
  | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/cran.list




Install R:


Install base packages:





Listing 3.26: Install R base


sudo apt update
sudo apt install r-base r-base-dev -y
R --version



ii. Install recommended Ubuntu system libraries for scientific
    computing and network/plotting support (@lst-r-syslibs):



Listing 3.27: System libraries for R packages


## Compilation tools
sudo apt install cmake

## Network, imaging, and plotting libraries
sudo apt install \
  build-essential \
  libpng-dev \
  libjpeg-dev \
  libtiff-dev \
  libcairo2-dev \
  libcurl4-openssl-dev \
  libssl-dev \
  libxml2-dev \
  zlib1g-dev

## Scientific libraries
sudo apt install \
  build-essential \
  gfortran \
  libblas-dev \
  liblapack-dev \
  libgsl-dev



<!-- -->

Configure a default CRAN mirror:


The official mirror https://cloud.r-project.org is the most up to date.
On Ubuntu, the Posit Package Manager mirror is often much faster because it serves prebuilt Linux binaries. Pin it in ~/.Rprofile (Listing 3.28), replacing <ubuntu-version> with your release (e.g. noble):





Listing 3.28: Posit Package Manager in ~/.Rprofile


echo 'options(repos = c(CRAN = "https://packagemanager.posit.co/cran/__linux__/<ubuntu-version>/latest"))' \
  >> ~/.Rprofile



<!-- -->

Install packages in a reproducible way (project lockfiles, renv, or a curated meta-package). Stephen Turner’s tidyverse-oriented stack is a useful starting set for many bioinformatics pipelines: remotes::install_github("stephenturner/Tverse", upgrade = TRUE).
Install Air, the recommended fast formatter for R, as a user-level CLI tool via uv (Listing 3.29). Configure Cursor (or your editor) to call air on save; see the Air documentation for editor integration.




Listing 3.29: Install Air formatter via uv


uv tool install air-formatter





3.11.2 Quarto
Install Quarto from the official site: https://quarto.org/docs/get-started/. Example local .deb install (Listing 3.30):



Listing 3.30: Install Quarto


sudo apt install ./quarto-1.3.496-linux-amd64.deb
quarto check



A minimal inline maths check:
\[
a = 10
\]


3.11.3 Cursor with R

Install the following R packages for language support, rendering, and debugging (Listing 3.31):

title: 3  Software to install
text:
3.12 Python

From PEP 668, on modern Debian/Ubuntu with a system Python of 3.11 or newer, pip is blocked from modifying the system Python so that it cannot break apt-managed packages.


This section evolves quickly. Prefer the uv-centric workflow below; treat older pip / Poetry / Conda advice as legacy unless you are constrained by an HPC site.


3.12.1 Modern Python guidelines






TipModern Python development guidelines






Recent Ubuntu releases (including Noble) strongly discourage installing extra system-wide Python interpreters. Avoid sudo apt install python3.14-full and Deadsnakes PPAs for day-to-day work.
uv replaces a cluster of slower, single-purpose tools (pip, poetry for many workflows, virtualenv, pipx, …) with a faster unified CLI — see Figure 3.7 and Figure 3.6. Poetry may still be preferable for some package-publishing edge cases; pip remains the legacy default on older HPC images.
For multi-language environments, pixi has largely superseded Conda/Mamba. Use uv for Python-centric projects; use pixi when you need non-Python dependencies in the same lockfile. Note that uv enforces virtual environments when running project scripts — see Table 3.1.
The ecosystem moves fast: reassess tooling yearly.

Table 3.1: Comparison of Python environment and dependency management tools

















(a) Each tool used to have its own perimeter, hence the diversity of Python executables











(b) The three levels of Python environments, from system-wide (do not modify) to the project level













(c) Side-by-side comparison of core use cases for each Python tool — uv covers most of them







Figure 3.6: Comparison of Python managers and environment layers.














(a) Main commands that replace older Python tools with uv











(b) Caricature of the recent dominance of uv











(c) Decision tree: uv for pure Python projects, Poetry (or uv) for packaging edge cases, and pixi for cross-language projects. Conda and Mamba are no longer required in a modern default stack.







Figure 3.7: uv as the default Python tooling layer.





3.12.2 One tool to bind them: a uv workflow
The steps below install a recent Python (example: 3.14) without replacing the system interpreter Ubuntu depends on.

Install uv:




Listing 3.33: Install uv


curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh




Install a managed Python with uv:




Listing 3.34: Install a Python version with uv


uv python install 3.14




Pin the Python version at one of two levels:


Project level: uv python pin 3.14.
User level:





Listing 3.35: User-level Python with uv


cd ~
echo "3.14" > ~/.python-version



<!-- -->

Prefer uv tool install (instead of pipx) for CLI utilities — formatters, notebook tools, hooks, and so on. As with pipx, these tools are added to the user PATH (Listing 3.36):




Listing 3.36: Install CLI tools with uv tool


uv tool install ruff
uv tool install "dvc[ssh]"   # data versioning when Git LFS is not enough
uv tool install black
uv tool install marimo       # preferred notebook / reactive Python UI
uv tool install ipython
uv tool install pre-commit
uv tool install cookiecutter # project templates for packaging
## optional legacy / niche tools:
# uv tool install jupyterlab
# uv tool install poetry









TipPython version management: core checks






Check the system Python:




Listing 3.37: Inspect system Python


ls /usr/bin/python* ## typically a single 3.12 on modern Ubuntu




Check versions managed by uv:




Listing 3.38: Inspect uv-managed Python


ls -la ~/.local/share/uv/python*
## paths should live under your HOME directory




Checking which Python is active:

From the terminal (system-wide), ls -d /usr/lib/python3.* or which -a python should point at the OS Python only when you intend to use it.
From a Python shell (or Marimo / optional Jupyter):




Listing 3.39: Python environment summary


import sys
print(sys.version)
print(sys.executable)
print(sys.path)




Useful reading:

From Pip to Lightning: How uv Opened My Eyes to Better Python Workflows
LinkedIn post on Python dependency managers






3.12.3 Marimo (preferred over Jupyter Lab)
Marimo is the recommended interactive notebook tool for this course: notebooks are plain Python files, reactive, and easy to version-control. Jupyter Lab remains available as an optional uv tool if a collaborator requires it.

Install Marimo with commonly used extras (DuckDB SQL cells, Polars / PyArrow, Ruff, Vegafusion charts):




Listing 3.40: Install Marimo via uv


uv tool install "marimo[recommended]"

# Verify
marimo --version




Add the Cursor / VS Code extension:




Listing 3.41: Install Marimo Cursor extension


cursor --install-extension marimo-team.vscode-marimo




Suggested keybindings (add to keybindings.json):




Listing 3.42: Suggested Marimo keybindings


// --- Marimo ---
// Open current .py file as a marimo notebook in the editor
{
  "key": "ctrl+alt+m",
  "command": "marimo.openNotebook",
  "when": "resourceExtname == '.py'"
},
// Create a new sandboxed marimo notebook via terminal
{
  "key": "ctrl+alt+shift+m",
  "command": "workbench.action.terminal.sendSequence",
  "args": { "text": "uvx marimo edit --sandbox \n" }
},
// Run current marimo notebook as a read-only app
{
  "key": "ctrl+alt+r",
  "command": "workbench.action.terminal.sendSequence",
  "when": "resourceExtname == '.py'",
  "args": { "text": "uvx marimo run '${file}'\n" }
}




An interactive example is provided in demo.py.

title: 3  Software to install
text:
3.16 Password manager: Bitwarden
Bitwarden is the recommended password manager on Linux for most teaching and research setups: it is largely free, works with major browsers (Firefox, Chrome, …), syncs across many devices, and stores more than passwords (passkeys, SSH secrets, payment cards). Lightweight mobile apps exist for iPhone and Android. It also covers Windows and Linux, which goes well beyond the local GNOME Passwords and Keys tool.
One limitation: it does not automatically flag duplicate entries as thoroughly as some commercial managers.
Follow the steps in Listing 3.478.



Listing 3.47: Install Bitwarden via Flatpak


## Install Flatpak and the GNOME Flatpak plugin
sudo apt install flatpak
sudo apt install gnome-software-plugin-flatpak

## Add the Flathub repository
flatpak remote-add --if-not-exists flathub \
  https://dl.flathub.org/repo/flathub.flatpakrepo

## Install and run Bitwarden locally
flatpak install flathub com.bitwarden.desktop
flatpak run com.bitwarden.desktop

## Install the browser add-on (Chrome example), then pin it:
## https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/bitwarden-password-manage/nngceckbapebfimnlniiiahkandclblb?hl=en

## Export, then import your password database from other browsers



In the Auto-fill settings, leave Do not auto-fill on page load unticked, and set Default URI matching to Exact to reduce ambiguous fills. Counter-intuitively, use the Bitwarden Web Vault for bulk deletion of entries; that workflow is not fully exposed in the desktop app.

title: 4  AMU tools and remote servers
text:
4.2 Working with a remote server
Prefer Cursor or VS Code with the Remote SSH extension for everyday remote development: the editor runs locally while the terminal, language servers, and compute run on the cluster. Avoid relying on hosted desktop IDEs or notebook servers on the cluster for routine work.2






NoteRetrieve your identity on the server








Listing 4.1: server id


id ${USER}
# Example (local-style groups):
# uid=1001(bastien) gid=1001(bastien) groups=1001(bastien),4(adm),...
#
# Example on the MMG cluster (project group):
# uid=1007(<your-username>) gid=1007(<your-username>) groups=1007(<your-username>),1043(<project-group>)



Identity on a Linux server is defined by the combination of username, UID (user ID), and GID (group ID), plus membership of project groups. More detail is available in the Server Management tutorial.




4.2.1 SSH configuration
The dual aim is to avoid typing your password on every connection and to keep a safe, reusable list of remote hosts.

Set up SSH remote access (key-based authentication). The remote machine needs openssh-server:




Listing 4.2: openssh server


## remote server must have openssh-server installed
sudo apt install openssh-server




Generate an Ed25519 public–private key pair on your local machine:3




Listing 4.3: ssh keygen


ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "your_email@example.com"



This creates:

~/.ssh/id_ed25519 (private key)
~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub (public key)


Copy your public key to the server with ssh-copy-id username@server_ip. After that, password login is no longer required for that host.
(Optional) Keep a ~/.ssh/config entry per cluster. Aliases such as ssh ifb-core then suffice, and the same file is what Cursor / VS Code Remote SSH uses to list hosts. Example:




Listing 4.4: ssh config


## Alias for the host connection: either "ifb-core" or "ifb"
Host ifb-core ifb

  ## The real hostname (or IP) of the remote server
  HostName core.cluster.france-bioinformatique.fr

  ## Username used on the remote machine
  User <your-ifb-username>

  ## Path to your private SSH key
  IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519

  ## Force SSH to use ONLY the key above
  IdentitiesOnly yes

  ## Authentication order: key, then keyboard-interactive, then password
  PreferredAuthentications publickey,keyboard-interactive,password

  ## Add this key to ssh-agent when used
  AddKeysToAgent yes

# Host configuration for the MMG cluster
Host mmg-sb-05 new-mmg-cluster
  HostName <mmg-server-hostname-or-ip>
  Port <non-default-ssh-port>  # prefer a non-22 port when the cluster provides one
  User <your-mmg-username>
  IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
  IdentitiesOnly yes
  PubkeyAuthentication yes
  PreferredAuthentications publickey,keyboard-interactive,password
  AddKeysToAgent yes
  ForwardX11 yes
  ForwardX11Trusted yes



A fuller host configuration (including default X11 forwarding) is available under config-ssh.






TipSSH configuration recommendations





On older Ubuntu setups, ssh-agent / ssh-add may not start by default. Enable the user service with systemctl --user enable --now ssh-agent.
See Table 4.1 and Figure 4.2 for a concise checklist and an overview of the first connection.










Practice
Why




Prefer Ed25519 keys
Small, fast, modern default.


Use a passphrase on the key
Protects the key if the disk is copied or stolen.


~/.ssh/config per host
Aliases and login options in one place.


Never commit private keys
Keep id_* out of Git and cloud-synced folders.


ssh-copy-id once per host
Standard way to populate authorized_keys.





Table 4.1: SSH recommended practices









Figure 4.2: Overview of an initial SSH connection














Option
Purpose
Effect on X11




-X
X11 forwarding (untrusted)
Runs GUI apps remotely


-Y
X11 forwarding (trusted)
Runs all GUI apps remotely


-C
Compression
Reduces network usage; can help GUI over slow links





Table 4.2: Main options for a customised ssh connection








4.2.2 MMG cluster and recommendations for project management
As soon as collaboration is involved, follow these project tips:

Initialise git and GitHub at the real start of the project.
Keep work under /mnt/<cluster-name>/projects/ only (nothing long-lived in your home directory except quick tests).
When creating the project, set group and user permissions carefully, following the guidelines in Server_Management.pdf, section Creating a New Project.
Maintain a README.md at the root of the projects tree with one short line per directory summarising the study’s overarching objective.

title: 5  R programming guidelines
text:
5.1 Package Structure
This guide consolidates package development practice using modern recommendations from the tidyverse ecosystem, especially R Packages (2nd edition) by Hadley Wickham and Jenny Bryan.
A standard R package typically contains:

title: 5  R programming guidelines
text:
R/: function source files (one primary function family per file).
man/: generated Rd help files (do not edit manually).
DESCRIPTION: package metadata and dependency declarations.
NAMESPACE: exports and imports, usually generated by roxygen2.
tests/testthat/: automated tests.
vignettes/: long-form user guides.
data/: user-facing datasets (.rda), loaded lazily when needed.
data-raw/: scripts that build derived datasets (not shipped to users directly).
inst/extdata/: raw or auxiliary files users may access via system.file().
src/: compiled code (for example C/C++), with LinkingTo when relevant.
.Rbuildignore: files excluded from package build.
.gitignore: files ignored by Git.
NEWS.md: notable user-facing changes.
README.Rmd and built README.md: project overview and installation instructions.

title: 5  R programming guidelines
text:
5.2 Project Setup (End-to-End)

Create the package project:
usethis::create_package("~/path/to/pkgname")
Validate naming conventions (letters, numbers, and . only; start with a letter).
Activate common infrastructure:
usethis::use_git()
usethis::use_github()
usethis::use_mit_license("Your Name")
usethis::use_readme_rmd()
usethis::use_news_md()
Add continuous checks early:
usethis::use_testthat(3)
usethis::use_github_action_check_standard()
During development, use fast feedback loops:
devtools::load_all()
devtools::test()
devtools::document()
devtools::check()

title: 5  R programming guidelines
text:
5.3 Writing Functions

Put package code in R/; avoid source() inside a package.
Do not call library() or require() in package code.
Prefer explicit namespace calls (pkg::fun) unless a function is imported repeatedly.
Keep side effects local; for temporary global option/state changes, use withr.
Use snake_case naming and tidyverse style conventions.

title: 5  R programming guidelines
text:
5.4 Dependencies and Namespaces
Use DESCRIPTION fields correctly:

Imports: packages required at runtime.
Suggests: optional packages used in tests, examples, or vignettes.
LinkingTo: headers needed for compiled code interfaces.
SystemRequirements: non-R system dependencies.

Recommended workflow:
usethis::use_package("dplyr", type = "Imports")
usethis::use_package("testthat", type = "Suggests")
In roxygen comments:

@export exposes functions to users.
@importFrom pkg fun imports specific functions where justified.

Prefer selective imports over broad @import directives.

title: 5  R programming guidelines
5  R programming guidelines
text:
5.6 Testing with testthat
Initialise and run tests:
usethis::use_testthat(3)
devtools::test()
Guidelines:

Store tests in tests/testthat/.
Name files as test-*.R.
Group related expectations in test_that() blocks.
Use the most specific matcher available (expect_identical(), expect_equal(), expect_match(), etc.).
Use snapshot/reference testing where outputs are large or complex.
Skip selectively (skip_if_not_installed(), skip_on_cran()) rather than disabling broad test suites.

title: 5  R programming guidelines
text:
5.7 Data in Packages
Use the right location for each data type:

data/: user-facing, documented datasets.
R/sysdata.rda: internal package data not exposed to users.
inst/extdata/: external files users can access via system.file().
data-raw/: scripts to build reproducible datasets.

Helpful commands:
usethis::use_data_raw()
usethis::use_data(my_dataset, overwrite = TRUE)
usethis::use_data(my_internal_object, internal = TRUE, overwrite = TRUE)
tools::checkRdaFiles()
Document datasets with roxygen @format and @source.

title: 5  R programming guidelines
text:
5.8 Build, Check, and Release
Before release:

Run devtools::check() locally and in CI.
Confirm no unintended notes/warnings/errors.
Keep NAMESPACE generated (do not hand-edit unless absolutely necessary).
Verify encoding and avoid non-ASCII issues for CRAN where possible.
Increment versions with semantic intent:
usethis::use_version("patch")
Maintain a clear NEWS.md.

For CRAN submission, follow current CRAN policies and perform final checks with devtools::check() and devtools::check(cran = TRUE).

title: 5  R programming guidelines
section: 5.9 Documenting Multiple Functions on One Help Page
text:
5.9 Documenting Multiple Functions on One Help Page
Default recommendation: one function family per file and one principal help topic per user concept.
Use:

@seealso and @family for cross-links across related pages.
@rdname when several functions should share one help page.
@describeIn for closely related variants/methods with a shared conceptual contract.

Example:
#' Basic arithmetic
#'
#' @param x,y Numeric vectors.
#' @name arith
NULL

#' @rdname arith
add <- function(x, y) x + y

#' @rdname arith
times <- function(x, y) x * y

title: 5  R programming guidelines
text:
5.10 Parallel Computing in R (Practical Notes)
Check available cores:
parallel::detectCores()
Local multicore workflows:

parallel::mclapply() (Unix-like systems).
foreach with %dopar% plus doParallel.
Use reproducible RNG streams for parallel simulations (for example RNGkind("L'Ecuyer-CMRG") with a fixed seed).

Cluster workflows (PSOCK clusters), local or remote:

Create cluster with parallel::makeCluster().
Export required objects via parallel::clusterExport() when needed.
Evaluate with parallel::parLapply() or related functions.
Stop cleanly using parallel::stopCluster().

Always close clusters and backend registrations to avoid orphan workers.

title: 5  R programming guidelines
text:
5.11 Lifecycle R development
The following diagrams summarise package construction, build, installation, and loading in an Excalidraw-like flow.

5.11.1 1) High-level package lifecycle





flowchart LR
    A["Source package<br/>editable files<br/>nothing compiled"] --> B["Bundle (tar.gz)<br/>single compressed archive<br/>distribution artefact"]
    B --> C["Binary package<br/>platform-specific build<br/>compiled where needed"]
    C --> D["Installed package<br/>copied into local library<br/>ready to attach or namespace-load"]
    D --> E["Loaded package in memory<br/>namespace loaded / attached<br/>functions available in session"]








5.11.2 2) What changes between source, bundle, and binary





flowchart LR
    subgraph S["Source"]
      S1["DESCRIPTION"]
      S2["NAMESPACE"]
      S3["README.md"]
      S4["man/"]
      S5["R/ (plain .R files)"]
      S6["src/"]
      S7["tests/"]
      S8["vignettes/"]
      S9["inst/"]
      S10["dev-only files<br/>.Rbuildignore, devtools config, CRAN notes"]
    end

    subgraph B["Bundle"]
      B1["DESCRIPTION"]
      B2["NAMESPACE"]
      B3["README.md"]
      B4["man/"]
      B5["R/"]
      B6["src/"]
      B7["tests/"]
      B8["inst/doc (built vignettes)"]
      B9["inst/"]
    end

    subgraph Y["Binary"]
      Y1["DESCRIPTION (+ parsed metadata cache)"]
      Y2["NAMESPACE"]
      Y3["README.md"]
      Y4["help system<br/>Meta/, html/, help/, INDEX"]
      Y5["R/ (lazy-load database)"]
      Y6["libs/ (compiled shared objects)"]
      Y7["doc/"]
      Y8["top-level files from inst/"]
    end

    S1 --> B1 --> Y1
    S2 --> B2 --> Y2
    S3 --> B3 --> Y3
    S4 --> B4 --> Y4
    S5 --> B5 --> Y5
    S6 --> B6 --> Y6
    S8 --> B8 --> Y7
    S9 --> B9 --> Y8








5.11.3 3) Command-driven workflow (construction to load)





flowchart TD
    A["Create scaffolding<br/>usethis::create_package()"] --> B["Write code + docs<br/>R/, roxygen comments"]
    B --> C["Generate docs + namespace<br/>devtools::document()"]
    C --> D["Run tests<br/>devtools::test()"]
    D --> E["Run full checks<br/>devtools::check()"]
    E --> F["Build source bundle<br/>devtools::build()"]
    F --> G["Install locally<br/>devtools::install()"]
    G --> H["Load in session<br/>library(pkg) or pkg::fun"]

text: A.1 Open-source installation for Ubuntu

title: Appendix A — OneDrive on Linux
text:
Install dependencies:



Listing A.1: onedrive deps


sudo apt install build-essential libcurl4-openssl-dev pkg-config git -y



Add the openSUSE Build Service repository release key:



Listing A.2: onedrive repo


wget -qO - https://download.opensuse.org/repositories/home:/npreining:/debian-ubuntu-onedrive/xUbuntu_24.04/Release.key | gpg --dearmor | sudo tee /usr/share/keyrings/obs-onedrive.gpg > /dev/null

echo "deb [arch=$(dpkg --print-architecture) signed-by=/usr/share/keyrings/obs-onedrive.gpg] https://download.opensuse.org/repositories/home:/npreining:/debian-ubuntu-onedrive/xUbuntu_24.04/ ./" | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/onedrive.list

## update cache
sudo apt-get update



Install OneDrive:



Listing A.3: onedrive install


sudo apt install --no-install-recommends --no-install-suggests onedrive



Sync OneDrive:

Exclude large folders and directories that are complex or not recommended for syncing: nano ~/.config/onedrive/config. See the contents of a working config under onedrive-custom-config.1
Authenticate, then run OneDrive once:



Listing A.4: onedrive sync


onedrive --sync --dry-run ## optional: list folders that will be synchronised
onedrive --sync --verbose ## first initialisation; usually time-consuming; one-shot

title: Appendix A — OneDrive on Linux
section: A.2 Permanent monitoring: pick exactly one path
text:
A.2 Permanent monitoring: pick exactly one path






Warning A.1



Do not run systemd monitoring and a OneDrive GUI / tray client at the same time. Concurrent clients fight over the same local tree and produce “already running” errors, stalled uploads, or silent conflicts. Choose either Listing A.5 or Tip A.1 — never both (Figure A.1).








flowchart TD
  A[Need continuous OneDrive sync?] --> B{Prefer terminal<br/>diagnostics?}
  B -->|Yes| C[Enable user systemd service]
  C --> D["systemctl --user enable --now onedrive"]
  D --> E["Monitor with journalctl --user-unit onedrive -f"]
  B -->|No| F[Install lightweight tray GUI]
  F --> G[onedrive_tray user service]
  G --> H[Status icon in the panel]
  C -.->|Do not combine| F
  E --> I[Single client owns the sync]
  H --> I




Figure A.1: Decision tree: systemd journal monitoring versus a tray GUI for OneDrive






A.2.1 Option A — systemd + journalctl



Listing A.5: onedrive systemd


systemctl --user enable onedrive
systemctl --user start onedrive ## backend equivalent: onedrive --monitor



Monitor uploads:



Listing A.6: onedrive monitor


journalctl --user-unit onedrive -f ## continuous; or systemctl --user status onedrive (one-shot)

onedrive --display-config
onedrive --version





A.2.2 Option B — tray GUI






Tip A.1: GUIs for OneDrive monitoring



OneDrive system tray program adds a simple icon that reports OneDrive synchronisation status.
If you use this path, disable the systemd user service first (systemctl --user disable --now onedrive) so only one client runs (see Warning A.1).



Listing A.7: onedrive tray


## install Qt 5 qmake
sudo apt install qt5-qmake qtbase5-dev

## build the executable
git clone https://github.com/DanielBorgesOliveira/onedrive_tray.git
cd onedrive_tray
mkdir build
cd build
/usr/lib/qt5/bin/qmake ../systray.pro ## prepare the Makefile
make ## build

## install so it runs at login
sudo make install ## deploy; sudo is required here
systemctl enable --user onedrive_tray.service











WarningGraphical interfaces for OneDrive



Avoid full graphical clients such as OneDriveGUI: in practice they often clash with a local onedrive install.
Prefer the terminal (Option A) or the lightweight tray icon (Option B in Tip A.1) for clearer control over configuration.

title: Appendix A — OneDrive on Linux
text:
A.3 Troubleshoot OneDrive

Call systemctl --user restart onedrive after modifying the config file so changes take effect (Option A). To re-apply configuration retrospectively, use onedrive --resync --sync --verbose sparingly. Synchronisation stops without warning when the config file changes; you must restart the service.
The warning “onedrive application is already running, please check process list” means several concurrent onedrive processes are running — almost always because systemd and a GUI were started together (Warning A.1):

List them: ps aux | grep onedrive
Stop the service and stray processes:



Listing A.8: Stop concurrent OneDrive clients


systemctl --user stop onedrive.service
pkill -f "onedrive --sync" || true
pkill -f "onedrive --monitor" || true
pgrep -af onedrive ## should return nothing before continuing






A.3.1 Safe recovery after a messy sync
When local and cloud trees have diverged badly, treat a restored local folder as the temporary source of truth, push it one-way, then return to two-way sync. Do not edit files on the web or locally while a sync or resync is running.

Stop every client (Listing A.8).
For a migration / upload-only phase, set in ~/.config/onedrive/config (adjust sync_dir to your restored tree):



Listing A.9: Temporary upload-only OneDrive config


skip_dir = "venv|\\.venv|__pycache__|node_modules|\\.next|renv|.cache"
skip_file = "\\.Rhistory$|\\.RData$|~*|.~*|*.tmp|*.swp|*.partial"
check_nosync = "true"
local_first = "true"
display_manager_integration = "true"
use_recycle_bin = "true"
force_session_upload = "true"
delay_inotify_processing = "true"
sync_dir = "~/OneDrive-restored"
upload_only = "true"
download_only = "false"



Resynchronise once (example background run):



Listing A.10: One-way upload resync


nohup onedrive --sync --resync --resync-auth --verbose \
  > "$HOME/onedrive-migration-resync.log" 2>&1 &



Switch back to normal two-way sync: move the restored tree to your usual path if needed (mv ~/OneDrive-restored ~/OneDrive), restore the sample settings from onedrive-custom-config (upload_only = "false"), then:



Listing A.11: Final two-way resync


onedrive --sync --resync --verbose



Re-enable exactly one monitoring path again (Warning A.1): either Listing A.5 or Tip A.1.







NoteOneDrive, Git and EOL encoding across OS





Git and OneDrive do not combine well when:

End-of-line encodings differ: Linux and macOS use LF (line feed: \n); Windows uses CRLF (carriage return + line feed: \r\n).
Linux tracks executable permissions; Windows does not (mainly an issue for shell scripts).
.git directories are complex repositories and are often a poor fit for cloud sync.


To avoid these issues:

Configure .gitconfig globally so both EOL styles are handled. Use git config --global core.autocrlf input on Linux and macOS when collaborating with Windows machines2, and git config --global core.autocrlf true on Windows3.
For extra robustness, add a per-project .gitattributes file4:



Listing A.12: onedrive gitattributes


## three columns: extension, type (text or binary), EOL for text files
*.sh   text eol=lf
*.py   text eol=lf
*.js   text eol=lf
*.ts   text eol=lf
*.java text eol=lf



Then apply the change with Git (this renormalises tracked files; rules in .gitattributes override the global core.autocrlf option):



Listing A.13: onedrive renormalize


git add --renormalize .
git status ## files affected by the EOL change
git commit -m "Normalize line endings"



Set the editor default end-of-line encoding:

-   *VS Code / Cursor*: , then “Open User
    Settings”, search for `Files: Eol`, and set end of line to `\n`.







Figure A.2: Best practices for end-of-line homogenisation across devices












WarningCompatibility with editors using atomic saves





Many editors — including LibreOffice, and often VS Code / Cursor when saving project files — use atomic save strategies to preserve data integrity: the editor writes a temporary file, then renames it over the original.



Listing A.14: onedrive atomic flow


file.qmd
↓ edit
file.qmd.tmp ## if OneDrive syncs mid-save, it may treat the file as discarded
↓ rename
file.qmd


## Architecture that causes the clash
Editor (LibreOffice, Cursor, …)
   │
   │ save (atomic)
   ▼
Local file
   │
   │ filesystem event (inotify)
   ▼
onedrive client
   │
   │ sync
   ▼
OneDrive cloud
   │
   │ sync back
   ▼
local overwrite



That pattern can interfere with the onedrive client’s inotify-based detection, producing editor warnings or briefly emptying file contents.
Three complementary approaches:

Keep active Git projects outside OneDrive. Use OneDrive for large document stores; keep source trees under Git elsewhere (or in a path excluded from sync).
Pause sync while editing intensively — and remember to restart synchronisation afterwards.
Adjust the config to tolerate atomic saves (already in onedrive-custom-config):



Listing A.15: onedrive atomic config


force_session_upload = "true" ## reduce overwrites by older cloud versions mid-save
delay_inotify_processing = "true" ## wait for tmp → rename to finish before syncing
